The design optimization of the HSCT engine was cast as a nonlinear optimization problem.
The merit function for the optimization was engine thrust.
The design variables included bypass ratios, fan r-values, fuel flow, and other factors.
Constraints were specified on factors such as maximum compressor speed, positive surge margins for compressors, discharge temperature, pressure ratios, and mixer Mach number.

The cascade optimization strategy was necessary because the most reliable optimization algorithm available in COMETBOARDS could only provide feasible optimum results for a portion of the aircraft flight regime.
The cascade optimization strategy used multiple optimizers in a specified sequence, pseudorandom damping, and reduction of the design space distortion via a global scaling scheme.
The cascade optimization strategy was able to converge to the same global optimum solution, even when initiated from different design points.
The HSCT engine concept that was optimized was a Mach-2.4 mixed-flow turbofan engine.
The optimum thrust of the HSCT engine concept, as determined by the COMETBOARDS solution, was normalized with respect to the NEPP results.
The COMETBOARDS tool was able to successfully solve a number of engine design problems for their flight regimes, which the most reliable optimization algorithm available could not do.
The cascade optimization strategy was crucial in solving this complex, multidisciplinary design problem.
The HSCT air-breathing propulsion system was designed for multimission, variable-cycle operations.
The NASA Engine Performance Program (NEPP) was used as the engine performance analyzer.
The COMETBOARDS tool was developed at the NASA Lewis Research Center.
The optimization problem had a large number of mission points, diverse constraint types, and overall poor conditioning of the design space.
